quotes: The numbers $(f, \varphi_k)$ are called Fourier coefficients of $f$ .

statement: The normalized Legendre polynomials phi_n = y_n/||y_n|| form the orthonormal sequence obtained by normalizing the Legendre orthogonalization output y_n.
quotes: are called the normalized Legendre polynomials.
given by $\varphi_{n} = y_{n}/\|y_{n}\|$ are called the normalized Legendre polynomials.

statement: An element in V is said to be orthogonal to a subset S if it is orthogonal to every element of S.
quotes: An element in V is said to be orthogonal to S if it is orthogonal to every element of S.

statement: The distance between two elements x and y of a Euclidean space is defined to be the norm of x - y.
quotes: The distance between two elements x and y is defined to be the norm

statement: If S is a subspace of a Euclidean space, the set S-perp of all elements orthogonal to S is called the orthogonal complement of S.
quotes: In case S is a subspace, then $S^{\perp}$ is called the orthogonal complement of S.

statement: Given a finite-dimensional subspace S of a Euclidean space V and an element x in V, the problem is to determine an element in S whose distance from x is as small as possible.
quotes: Given an element x in V, to determine an element in S whose distance from x is as small as possible.

statement: Each term (x,ei)ei is the projection of x along ei, and the projection s is the sum of the projections of x along each basis element.
quotes: Note that each term $(x, e_{i})e_{i}$ is the projection of x along $e_{i}$
The element s is the sum of the projections of x along each basis element.

statement: Theorem 15.16. If S is a finite-dimensional subspace of a Euclidean space V and x is any element of V, then the projection s of x on S is nearer to x than any other element of S: ||x - s|| <= ||x - t|| for all t in S.
quotes: THEOREM 15.16. APPROXIMATION THEOREM. Let S be a finite-dimensional subspace of a Euclidean space V, and let x be any element of V.
Then the projection of x on S is nearer to x than any other element of S.

statement: Relative to an orthonormal basis {e1,...,en} of S, the projection of x on S is given by s = sum from i=1 to n of (x,ei) ei.

Theorem 15.13, the Orthogonalization Theorem: for any finite or infinite sequence x_1, x_2, ... in a Euclidean space V there is a corresponding sequence y_1, y_2, ... such that (a) each y_k is orthogonal to L(y_1,...,y_{k-1}), (b) L(y_1,...,y_k)=L(x_1,...,x_k), and (c) the sequence is unique except for scalar factors.
quotes: THEOREM 15.13. ORTHOGONALIZATION THEOREM. Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots,$ be a finite or infinite sequence of elements in a Euclidean space $V$
(a) The element $y_{k}$ is orthogonal to every element in the subspace $L(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{k - 1})$ .

statement: The Legendre polynomials P_n arise when the orthogonalization theorem is applied to the sequence x_n(t)=t^n under the inner product (x,y)=int_{-1}^1 x(t)y(t)dt; they are scalar multiples of the orthogonalized polynomials y_n.
quotes: are known as the Legendre polynomials.
first encountered by the French mathematician A. M. Legendre (1752–1833) in his work on potential theory.

statement: The Gram-Schmidt process: an iterative construction that starts with y_1 = x_1 and, having built y_1,...,y_r, forms the next element by subtracting from x_{r+1} its projections onto the earlier y_i, producing an orthogonal set of nonzero elements spanning the same subspace as an independent set x_1,...,x_k.
quotes: These formulas describe the Gram-Schmidt process for constructing an orthogonal set of nonzero elements $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{k}$
We construct the elements $y_1, y_2, \ldots$ , by induction. To start the process, we take $y_1 = x_1$ .
The construction is called the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process, in honor of J. P. Gram

statement: The explicit Gram-Schmidt formulas (15.15): y_1 = x_1 and y_{r+1} = x_{r+1} - sum_{i=1}^r ((x_{r+1},y_i)/(y_i,y_i)) y_i for r = 1,...,k-1, valid when the x_i are independent so each y_i is nonzero.
quotes: the coefficients $a_{i}$ in (15.13) are given by (15.14), and the formulas defining $y_{1},\ldots,y_{k}$ become
y _ {1} = x _ {1}, \quad y _ {r + 1} = x _ {r + 1} - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \frac {\left(x _ {r + 1} , y _ {i}\right)}{\left(y _ {i} , y _ {i}\right)} y _ {i}

statement: Theorem 15.14: every finite-dimensional Euclidean space has an orthonormal basis. It follows as a corollary of Theorem 15.13 by normalizing each element of an orthogonal basis.
quotes: THEOREM 15.14. Every finite-dimensional Euclidean space has an orthonormal basis.
We can also convert this to an orthonormal basis by normalizing each element $y_{i}$ , that is, by dividing it by its norm.

statement: Property (c) of the orthogonalization theorem: the sequence y_1, y_2, ... is unique except for scalar factors; any other sequence satisfying (a) and (b) has y_k' = c_k y_k for some scalar c_k.
quotes: (c) The sequence $y_1, y_2, \ldots$ , is unique, except for scalar factors.
then for each $k$ there is a scalar $c_k$ such that $y_k' = c_k y_k$ .

statement: For elements x and y in a Euclidean space with y != O, the element ((x,y)/(y,y)) y is called the projection of x along y; the Gram-Schmidt process forms each new vector by subtracting such projections.
quotes: is called the projection of x along y.

statement: Let S be a finite-dimensional subspace of a Euclidean space V with orthonormal basis {e1,...,en}. For x in V, the element s = sum (x,ei) ei is called the projection of x on the subspace S.
quotes: is called the projection of $x$ on the subspace $S$
Let $S$ be a finite-dimensional subspace of a Euclidean space $V$ , and let $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ be an orthonormal basis for $S$

statement: For any subset S of a Euclidean space V, S-perp is a subspace of V, whether or not S itself is a subspace.
quotes: It is a simple exercise to verify that $S^{\perp}$ is a subspace of V, whether or not S itself is one.

statement: The problem of approximating a given element x of a Euclidean space V by elements of a finite-dimensional subspace S, i.e. finding the element of S that is nearest to x in norm.
quotes: Best approximation of elements in a Euclidean space by elements in a finite-dimensional subspace

statement: Every finite-dimensional Euclidean space has an orthogonal basis: if x_1,...,x_k is a basis for a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, then the Gram-Schmidt output y_1,...,y_k is an orthogonal basis for the same space.
quotes: If the space is Euclidean, we can always construct an orthogonal basis.
In particular, if $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}$ is a basis for a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, then $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{k}$ is an orthogonal basis for the same space.

statement: Property (b) of the orthogonalization theorem: the subspace spanned by y_1,...,y_k is the same as the subspace spanned by x_1,...,x_k, i.e. L(y_1,...,y_k)=L(x_1,...,x_k).
quotes: (b) The subspace spanned by $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{k}$ is the same as that spanned by $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}$ :
L \left(y _ {1}, \dots , y _ {k}\right) = L \left(x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {k}\right).

statement: For the orthogonal decomposition x = s + s-perp, the norm of x is given by ||x||^2 = ||s||^2 + ||s-perp||^2.
quotes: Moreover, the norm of $x$ is given by the Pythagorean formula

statement: Theorem 15.15: Let V be a Euclidean space and S a finite-dimensional subspace of V. Then every element x in V can be represented uniquely as x = s + s-perp with s in S and s-perp in S-perp, and the norm satisfies the Pythagorean formula.
quotes: THEOREM 15.15. ORTHOGONAL DECOMPOSITION THEOREM. Let V be a Euclidean space and let S be a finite-dimensional subspace of V.
Then every element x in V can be represented uniquely as a sum of two elements, one in S and one in $S^{\perp}$

statement: An element of the (2n+1)-dimensional subspace S spanned by the orthonormal trigonometric functions phi_0, phi_1, ..., phi_{2n}.
quotes: span a subspace $S$ of dimension $2n + 1$ .
The elements of $S$ are called trigonometric polynomials.

statement: Example 2. The projection f_n of a continuous function f on the subspace of polynomials of degree <= n spanned by the normalized Legendre polynomials; it is the polynomial of degree <= n for which ||f - f_n|| is smallest.
quotes: EXAMPLE 2. Approximation of continuous functions on $[-1, 1]$ by polynomials of degree $\leq n$ .
This is the polynomial of degree $\leq n$ for which the norm $\| f - f_n\|$ is smallest.

statement: The element of the subspace S nearest to x in norm; it equals the projection of x on S, minimizes ||x - t|| over t in S, and is unique (equality holds if and only if t is the projection).
quotes: the equality sign holds if and only if $t = s$ .

statement: The representation of an element x as a sum x = s + s-perp of a component s lying in the subspace S and a component s-perp lying in S-perp, where s-perp = x - s.
quotes: x = s + s ^ {\perp}, \quad \text { where } \quad s \in S \quad \text { and } \quad s ^ {\perp} \in S ^ {\perp}.
s ^ {\perp} = x - s.

statement: Example 1. The projection f_n of a continuous function f on the subspace of trigonometric polynomials; it approximates f better than any other trigonometric polynomial in S, making ||f - f_n|| as small as possible.
quotes: EXAMPLE 1. Approximation of continuous functions on $[0, 2\pi]$ by trigonometric polynomials.
the trigonometric polynomial in (15.22) approximates f better than any other trigonometric polynomial in S, in the sense that the norm $\|f - f_{n}\|$ is as small as possible.

statement: The set of all elements orthogonal to a set S is denoted by S-perp and is called "S perpendicular".
quotes: The set of all elements orthogonal to S is denoted by $S^{\perp}$
